profile.address: 340, Cumberland Avenue, Parkside, West End, Portland, Cumberland County, Maine, 04101
profile.reading:
This record identifies a facility branded as FirstLight Data Center on Cumberland Avenue in Portland, Maine's Parkside and West End neighborhood, an area that mixes older commercial buildings with residential streets a short distance from downtown Portland and the peninsula's fiber and telecom infrastructure. FirstLight, the operator on file, is a regional fiber network and data center company headquartered at 12 Metro Park Road in Albany, New York. The company states on its own site that it has more than 25 years of history in the fiber and communications industry, operates a fiber network of roughly 20,000 route miles connecting more than 16,000 on net locations across the Northeast and mid Atlantic, and counts more than 15,000 businesses among its customers. FirstLight's business combines dark and lit fiber transport and internet access with colocation and data center space for enterprise, carrier, healthcare, education, and government customers who need physical infrastructure close to where their networks terminate.

Portland is one of several Maine markets where FirstLight maintains a presence, alongside the company's larger and more thoroughly documented facility in Brunswick, about 25 miles up the coast, which occupies a former NATO command and control building at the decommissioned Brunswick Naval Air Station. FirstLight expanded in Maine partly through acquisition, having absorbed Oxford Networks, a Maine based fiber and data center operator, after Oak Hill Capital Partners combined the two companies around 2017.

For the Cumberland Avenue address specifically, FirstLight's public pages describing named data center locations did not return a working facility page during this review, and no square footage, power capacity, cooling architecture, or Tier certification for this Portland site could be confirmed from the operator's own materials or from trade press coverage of the Brunswick facility, which covers a separate building entirely. That gap is worth noting on its own: FirstLight publishes detailed specifications for some of its data center locations, including Brunswick, but appears to treat others, including Portland, primarily as network access points or smaller colocation nodes rather than flagship facilities warranting a dedicated marketing page. Absent that documentation, what can be said with confidence is limited to the address, the operator's identity, and the operator's regional scale and history, rather than the physical characteristics of this particular building. A reader looking for rack density, generator capacity, or a tenant list for this specific Portland site will not find it published, which distinguishes this location from FirstLight's more prominently marketed sites.

profile.address: 14, Resilient Circle, Brunswick, Cumberland County, Maine, 04011
profile.reading:
The data center at 14 Resilient Circle in Brunswick, Maine occupies a building with an unusual history. It was built to serve as a NATO Command and Control Center at what was then Brunswick Naval Air Station, a Navy base whose airfield dates to 1935 and which operated as an active naval air station from 1943 until its decommissioning in 2011. When the Navy left, the base and its buildings were redeveloped as Brunswick Landing, a mixed use business park, and the former NATO command building was converted into a commercial data center around 2011 by Oxford Networks, a Maine based fiber and data center company, working with a partner identified in trade press coverage as Resilient Tier V. Oxford Networks expanded the facility again in 2014.

Ownership changed again around 2017, when Oak Hill Capital Partners, a private equity firm, combined Oxford Networks with FirstLight, the fiber network operator now listed as this facility's operator, which explains why a building associated with the Oxford Networks name in this record is now run under the FirstLight brand. FirstLight has continued to invest in the site. According to Data Center Dynamics, the company began a renovation in the summer of 2024 that doubled the facility's power capacity by 2025, installing dual independent 750 kilowatt generators for a combined 1.5 megawatts of standby generation, and outfitting the space for liquid cooled racks running at densities of roughly 12 to 15 kilowatts per rack, a density that supports higher performance computing workloads than typical air cooled colocation space. FirstLight has positioned the expanded Brunswick facility as both a disaster recovery site and a primary application hosting site for customers across the eastern United States, one of 14 data centers the company operates across Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New York, Pennsylvania, and Vermont.

What the public record does not establish is the building's total square footage, its formal Uptime Institute Tier certification if any, or a list of current tenants. The facility's military and NATO origin, its location inside a redeveloped naval air station, and its documented 2024 to 2025 power expansion are unusually well corroborated for a building of this kind, a product of Brunswick Landing's own redevelopment history and of trade press interest in a former NATO facility's second life as commercial data center infrastructure.

reading.body:
FirstLight operates two data centers in Maine as a secondary business line within a regional fiber network, not as a dedicated colocation platform, which means its facility footprint reflects network infrastructure acquisition rather than data center market expansion.

FirstLight's core business is a 20,000 route-mile fiber network across the Northeast and mid-Atlantic connecting over 16,000 on-net locations. The company added its two Maine facilities through acquisition of Maine Fiber Company in 2019. Data center colocation serves customers of that fiber network, including K-12 education, government, banking, healthcare, and hyperscalers, but does not anchor FirstLight's strategy the way colocation anchors operators like Equinix or CoreSite.

This positioning matters for understanding regional compute availability. FirstLight's Maine facilities exist to serve network customers seeking edge colocation near the fiber handoff, not to compete nationally for hyperscaler workloads. The company holds no published capacity figures for either facility, making it impossible to assess how much compute infrastructure these locations actually support. The data also does not cover whether FirstLight has pursued upgrades to its Maine facilities to meet rising power demands from AI workloads, or whether its fiber network bandwidth scales to modern requirements.
